document_order.text: Multimodal Disaster Relief Resource Mapping System
Course: CS Machine Learning Final Project  |  Northeastern University

DisasterLens is a multimodal AI system that takes disaster zone photos and news text snippets as input and produces a structured relief assessment: damage severity, estimated resource needs, and an interactive priority map for first responders.
The project is divided into four modules across two team members:
Download, clean, and explore AIDER and CrisisMMD datasets
Remap labels, analyze class distributions, prepare train/val/test splits
Classify damage severity from images using CLIP fine-tuning
Extract resource types via RoBERTa classification on text snippets
Output structured JSON per text input
Combine both JSONs, generate resource priority summary, render interactive map
Your three modules form the data backbone of the entire system. The quality of the final output depends directly on how well the Vision and NLP modules perform — this is where the core ML work lives.
Here is the full data flow end-to-end:
|-----> [NLP Module]    ->  { resources, location, population } <- YOUR WORK
└-----> [Fusion Layer]  ->  local entity extraction -> resource vector + summary
You own everything that feeds into the Fusion Layer. Your outputs are what determine the accuracy and usefulness of the final system — the fusion layer is only as good as what you pass into it.

This is the most important section. Both your modules must output exactly this JSON structure. Do not add extra fields or rename keys — the fusion layer depends on these exact field names to function correctly.
"severity": "severe",        // one of: none | mild | moderate | severe
"location": "Kathmandu, Nepal",                // string, null if not found
NOTE: If a field cannot be extracted, return null — never omit the key. The downstream code checks for key existence, not value.
Full name: Aerial Image Dataset for Emergency Response
Size: ~4,000 images across 5 categories: fire, flood, collapsed building, traffic accident, normal
Label remapping to our 4 severity levels:
collapsed building / severe flood -> severity: severe
Split into 80% train / 10% val / 10% test — stratified by class
EDA to include: class distribution bar chart, sample images per class, image size distribution
NOTE: The 5 AIDER categories don't map 1:1 to our 4 levels. Use the mapping above and adjust if you see heavy class imbalance after remapping.
Full name: CrisisMMD: Multimodal Twitter Datasets During Natural Disasters
Download: https://crisismmD.github.io or search 'CrisisMMD dataset download'
Size: ~18,000 tweets + images from 7 disasters (Harvey, Irma, Maria, Iraq earthquake, Mexico earthquake, Sri Lanka floods, California wildfires)
Labels available: informativeness, humanitarian category (infrastructure damage, rescue ops, affected individuals, etc.)
Map humanitarian categories to our resource types:
EDA to include: disaster type distribution, label balance, tweet length histogram, sample texts per category

Take a single image of a disaster zone and classify it into one of four damage severity levels: none, mild, moderate, severe. Output the JSON from Section 3.1.

Use OpenAI's CLIP model (ViT-B/32) as your base. It is pretrained on image-text pairs so it already understands visual concepts like 'flooded street' or 'collapsed building'. You only need to fine-tune the classification head on top.

5.3 Alternative: Zero-shot CLIP (if time is tight)
If fine-tuning takes too long, CLIP supports zero-shot classification using text prompts — no training needed:
text_inputs = [f'a disaster photo showing {l}' for l in labels]
# Compute cosine similarity between image embedding and each text label
NOTE: Zero-shot will get ~60-70% accuracy vs ~80-85% for fine-tuned. Fine-tuning is strongly preferred for the report — use zero-shot only as a fallback.
Per-class precision, recall, F1 — use sklearn.metrics.classification_report
Confusion matrix — use seaborn heatmap, screenshot for the report
3-5 example predictions with image + predicted label + confidence

Take a short news snippet or social media post about a disaster and extract structured information: which resource types are needed, location, population estimate, event type, and urgency keywords. Output the JSON from Section 3.2.

Fine-tune RoBERTa for multi-label classification to identify which of the four resource types (food, water, shelter, medical) are relevant in a given text. This is the core ML component of your NLP module.
pip install transformers torch scikit-learn datasets
Step 2: Load RoBERTa and set up multi-label classifier
# Map CrisisMMD humanitarian categories to our 4 resource types
# vehicle_damage -> []  (no resource match, label as empty)
# Each sample gets a binary vector: [food, water, shelter, medical]
# e.g. [1, 1, 0, 0] means food and water needed
# Threshold: 0.5 on sigmoid output to get binary predictions
Step 5: Prediction function (must match JSON contract)
return [resource_map[i] for i, p in enumerate(probs) if p > 0.5]
For location, population estimate, event type, and urgency keywords, use deterministic local extraction rules:
event_type = next((e for e in ('earthquake', 'flood', 'fire', 'hurricane') if e in lower), None)
location = location_match.group(1) if location_match else None
urgency_keywords = [term for term in urgent_terms if term in lower]
Resource classification: precision, recall, F1 per resource type
Entity extraction: manually evaluate 20-30 examples, report % correct per field
Show 3-5 example input/output pairs — include at least one failure case

n = analyze_text('Heavy flooding in Dhaka. 10,000 people displaced, need food.')
assert 'location' in n and 'population_estimate' in n

document_order.text: You are responsible for writing the following sections of the final report:
Dataset / Inputs — describe AIDER and CrisisMMD, label distributions, preprocessing steps, train/val/test split rationale
Methods: Vision Module — CLIP architecture, fine-tuning approach, label remapping decisions
Methods: NLP Module — RoBERTa setup, classification approach, and deterministic entity extraction
Results: Vision — accuracy, confusion matrix, per-class F1 with analysis
Results: NLP — resource classification metrics, entity extraction examples
AI Prompts Used — state whether any external prompts were used (required for grading)
NOTE: Mahek will compile the final document, write Introduction, Discussion, and the app demo section. Share your drafted sections by end of Week 5.
